fuentes/codice-boturini/soporte.texto: Strip of amate paper more than five meters long, folded like a screen (National Museum of Anthropology, Mexico)

fuentes/codice-boturini/resumen.texto: Pictographic account, without alphabetic text, of the migration of the Mexica from Aztlán: the departure guided by Huitzilopochtli, the stations along the route with their dates in Indigenous calendar years, and the conflicts along the way, up to their arrival in the Valley of Mexico and their subjugation at Culhuacán. Scholars debate whether it was painted shortly before or shortly after the conquest; its style, almost free of European influence, places it close to the pre-Hispanic tradition.

fuentes/codice-boturini/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the oldest surviving versions of the official Mexica account of their origins, which presents the Mexica as a people guided by their god toward a promised land.

fuentes/codice-azcatitlan/idioma_origina.texto: Nahua pictography with glosses in Nahuatl

fuentes/codice-azcatitlan/soporte.texto: Manuscript on European paper (National Library of France)

fuentes/codice-azcatitlan/resumen.texto: Pictographic history of the Mexica from the departure from Aztlán, the founding of Tenochtitlan and the reigns of the tlatoque, up to the arrival of the Spaniards, who appear accompanied by Malintzin, and the first colonial years. It is incomplete and its date is debated.

fuentes/codice-azcatitlan/por_que_import.texto: It shows how Nahua painters of the 16th century organized their own dynastic history and depicted the arrival of the Spaniards.

fuentes/codice-mendoza/autor.texto: Nahua painters and a Spanish interpreter (anonymous)

fuentes/codice-mendoza/idioma_original.texto: Nahua pictography with glosses and commentary in Spanish

fuentes/codice-mendoza/soporte.texto: Manuscript of 71 leaves on European paper (Bodleian Library, Oxford)

fuentes/codice-mendoza/resumen.texto: Commissioned around 1541, according to tradition by Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza for the king, it has three parts: the history of the tlatoque of Tenochtitlan and the peoples each one conquered; the list of tribute that about 400 towns, grouped into 38 provinces, delivered (mantles, cacao, feathers, gold, warrior costumes, foodstuffs); and the life of the Mexica from birth, with the education and punishments of children, marriage, the career of the warrior according to the captives he took, and trades. French corsairs captured it at sea, it passed through the hands of the cosmographer André Thevet, and it reached Oxford in the 17th century.

fuentes/codice-mendoza/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most complete source on the tribute of the Triple Alliance and on everyday Mexica life, although it was made after the conquest and for Spanish readers.

fuentes/codice-mendoza/leer.0.titulo.texto: Digital edition by the INAH, with facsimile and reading

fuentes/matricula-de-tributos/idioma_ori.texto: Nahua pictography with glosses in Nahuatl and Spanish

fuentes/matricula-de-tributos/soporte.texto: Sheets of amate paper (National Museum of Anthropology, Mexico)

fuentes/matricula-de-tributos/resumen.texto: Pictographic register of the tribute paid by the provinces subjected to the Triple Alliance, with the glyphs of the towns and the quantities of each product. Scholars debate whether it predates the conquest or dates from the first colonial years; it has glosses added later, and its content largely coincides with the second part of the Codex Mendoza.

fuentes/matricula-de-tributos/por_que_im.texto: It is the document closest to the tribute records of the Mexica administration itself.

fuentes/codice-aubin/titulo.texto: Aubin Codex (History of the Mexican Nation)

fuentes/codice-aubin/soporte.texto: Small book on European paper (British Museum)

fuentes/codice-aubin/resumen.texto: Annals in Nahuatl, with paintings, running from the departure from Aztlán to the early 17th century, with additions by several hands. They record the migration, the reigns, the arrival of the Spaniards and the massacre at the Toxcatl festival of 1520 year by year; the massacre is illustrated with a widely reproduced image. The annals then continue with the life of the colonial city.

fuentes/codice-aubin/por_que_importa.texto: It shows how the Nahuas kept writing their annals after the conquest, in their own language and with their own chronology.

fuentes/anales-de-tlatelolco/soporte.texto: Manuscript on European paper (National Library of France)

fuentes/anales-de-tlatelolco/resumen.texto: A set of texts in Nahuatl, written in the Latin alphabet, on the history of Tlatelolco and the conquest. The account of the siege, told from the side of the defeated, describes hunger, brackish water, and food made of adobe, lizards, mice and worms. It dates itself to 1528, which would make it one of the earliest writings in Nahuatl; several researchers believe the surviving manuscript is a somewhat later copy. It also tells that, after the fall, three wise men of Texcoco who surrendered with their painted books were thrown to the dogs in Coyoacán.

fuentes/anales-de-tlatelolco/por_que_imp.texto: It is the oldest surviving Indigenous testimony on the fall of Tenochtitlan, told from Tlatelolco, rival of the Tenochca.

fuentes/lienzo-de-tlaxcala/idioma_origin.texto: Nahua pictography with glosses in Nahuatl

fuentes/lienzo-de-tlaxcala/soporte.texto: The original, a large painted cloth, was lost; it is known through copies and fragments

fuentes/lienzo-de-tlaxcala/resumen.texto: Painting commissioned by the Indigenous cabildo of Tlaxcala, which depicts in dozens of scenes the alliance with Cortés, the baptism of the lords, the march to Tenochtitlan, La Noche Triste and the later campaigns in which the Tlaxcalans accompanied the Spaniards, as far as Guatemala and the west. It shows Malintzin at the center of the negotiations and Tlaxcalan warriors fighting side by side with the Spaniards.

fuentes/lienzo-de-tlaxcala/por_que_impor.texto: It is Tlaxcala's visual argument, presented before the Crown, in defense of its privileges as an ally: an Indigenous source with its own interests, which contradicts the image of a conquest carried out by Spaniards alone.

fuentes/historia-de-las-indias-duran/tit.texto: History of the Indies of New Spain and the Islands of Tierra Firme

fuentes/historia-de-las-indias-duran/sop.texto: Illustrated manuscript (National Library of Spain); not published until 1867–1880

fuentes/historia-de-las-indias-duran/res.texto: Work in three treatises: the history of the Mexica from the migration to the conquest, the book of the gods and rites, and the calendar. The historical part follows a Nahua chronicle that is now lost, the so-called Crónica X, and narrates in detail the wars, the coronations and the sacrifices of captives, among them the 80,400 he attributes to the dedication of the Templo Mayor in 1487. Durán wrote so that the friars would recognize what remained of the ancient religion.

fuentes/historia-de-las-indias-duran/por.texto: Together with Tezozómoc, it is the main source on the political history of Tenochtitlan as told from the tradition of its nobility; its figures for victims are debated.

fuentes/historia-de-las-indias-duran/lee.texto: 1867 edition by José Fernando Ramírez, volume 1, on the Internet Archive

fuentes/codice-tovar/titulo.texto: Tovar Codex (Account of the Origin of the Indians Who Inhabit This New Spain)

fuentes/codice-tovar/soporte.texto: Manuscript with about fifty paintings (John Carter Brown Library, Providence)

fuentes/codice-tovar/resumen.texto: Illustrated account of Mexica history, festivals and calendar, written by the Jesuit Juan de Tovar from the same tradition followed by Durán and Tezozómoc. Its paintings, by Indigenous hands, show the tlatoque, the gods and the rites, among them the sacrifice on the stone.

fuentes/codice-tovar/por_que_importa.texto: It was one of the routes by which Mexica history reached Europe, because José de Acosta summarized it in his Natural and Moral History of the Indies (1590).

fuentes/cronica-mexicana-tezozomoc/resum.texto: History of Tenochtitlan from its founding to the arrival of Cortés, written by a grandson of Moctezuma II using the same Nahua source that Durán used. It narrates the reigns, the wars of the Triple Alliance, the imposition of tribute and the sacrificial ceremonies, with many names and speeches, from the point of view of the Tenochca nobility.

fuentes/cronica-mexicana-tezozomoc/por_q.texto: It is the most extensive version of the official history of Tenochtitlan, written by a descendant of its rulers.

fuentes/cronica-mexicayotl/soporte.texto: Known through Chimalpahin's copy, with his additions

fuentes/cronica-mexicayotl/resumen.texto: Nahuatl chronicle on the origin of the Mexica, their migration, the founding of Tenochtitlan and the genealogies of their rulers up to the early 17th century. It is attributed to Tezozómoc, but survives in a copy by Chimalpahin, who expanded it, and the share of each is debated.

fuentes/cronica-mexicayotl/por_que_impor.texto: It is one of the main Nahuatl sources on the Tenochca dynasty and its continuity in the colonial nobility.

fuentes/historia-chichimeca/resumen.texto: History of the peoples of the Valley of Mexico, from the Toltecs and the Chichimecs of Xólotl to the conquest, centered on Texcoco. It presents Nezahualcóyotl as a lawgiver and poet who supposedly worshipped a single god, and Ixtlilxóchitl II as Cortés's decisive ally; it is based on Texcocan codices such as the Xólotl and on the testimony of elders.

fuentes/historia-chichimeca/por_que_impo.texto: It is the main source on the history of Texcoco, written by a descendant of its rulers who sought recognition and idealized his ancestors.

fuentes/relaciones-de-chimalpahin/autor.texto: Chimalpahin (Domingo Francisco de San Antón Muñón Chimalpahin Cuauhtlehuanitzin)

fuentes/relaciones-de-chimalpahin/resume.texto: Eight accounts in Nahuatl, in the form of annals, on the history of the lordships of Chalco and Amecameca, of Tenochtitlan and of other towns of the Valley of Mexico, from the migrations to the early 17th century. Chimalpahin compared codices and oral accounts and recorded the Mexica wars against Chalco from the Chalca point of view.

fuentes/relaciones-de-chimalpahin/por_qu.texto: It is one of the largest works written in Nahuatl and shows the history of central Mexico from the perspective of a people subjected by the Mexica.

fuentes/historia-de-tlaxcala-munoz-camar.texto: History of Tlaxcala (and Description of the City and Province of Tlaxcala)
The Description, with more than 150 drawings, is at the University of Glasgow; the History was published in 1892

Two versions of a history of Tlaxcala written by a mestizo of the city: the Description, prepared around 1580–1585 for the questionnaire of the relaciones geográficas and presented to Philip II, and the longer History. They deal with the origin of the Tlaxcalans, their government of four cabeceras, their wars with the Mexica, the alliance with Cortés, evangelization, and Tlaxcala's services to the Crown.
They set out the Tlaxcalan version of the conquest, written to defend the city's privileges.
History of Tlaxcala, edition by Alfredo Chavero (1892), on the Internet Archive

fuentes/relacion-de-texcoco-pomar/resume.texto: Reply to the questionnaire of the relaciones geográficas about Texcoco, describing its government, laws, religion, temples and sacrifices before the conquest, the education of young people, and the changes that followed the arrival of the Spaniards.

fuentes/relacion-de-texcoco-pomar/por_qu.texto: It is a description of Texcoco written by a descendant of its nobility, with information not found in other sources.

fuentes/codice-xolotl/soporte.texto: Sheets of amate paper (National Library of France)

fuentes/codice-xolotl/resumen.texto: Pictographic history of the Chichimecs of Xólotl and of the Texcoco dynasty, in the form of maps of the Valley of Mexico with figures, glyphs and dates, up to the war against Azcapotzalco in the time of Nezahualcóyotl. It was one of the sources of Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxóchitl.

fuentes/codice-xolotl/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the Texcocan historical tradition in its pictographic form, independent of the Tenochca version.

fuentes/cantares-mexicanos/soporte.texto: Manuscript in the National Library of Mexico

fuentes/cantares-mexicanos/resumen.texto: The largest collection of Nahuatl songs, gathered in the 16th century, probably in the circle of the Franciscans. It includes war songs, flower songs and songs of lament, some attributed to Nezahualcóyotl and other lords, and colonial-era songs with Christian themes. Ángel María Garibay and Miguel León-Portilla read them as pre-Hispanic poetry; John Bierhorst interpreted them as colonial-era ritual songs to summon the dead warriors.

fuentes/cantares-mexicanos/por_que_impor.texto: They are the main basis of what is known as Nahuatl poetry and of the image of Nezahualcóyotl as a poet, although the attributions are uncertain.

fuentes/codice-magliabechiano/idioma_ori.texto: Nahua pictography with commentary in Spanish

fuentes/codice-magliabechiano/soporte.texto: Manuscript on European paper (National Central Library of Florence)

fuentes/codice-magliabechiano/resumen.texto: Illustrated book on the ritual calendar, festivals, gods and customs of the Nahuas of central Mexico, a copy of a lost original. It includes scenes of sacrifice in the temple and a widely reproduced one of ritual cannibalism, with commentary in Spanish.

fuentes/codice-magliabechiano/por_que_im.texto: It contains some of the images of sacrifice and ritual cannibalism made in the 16th century by Indigenous painters, although they were annotated for Spanish readers.

fuentes/codice-telleriano-remensis/idiom.texto: Nahua pictography with commentary in Spanish

fuentes/codice-telleriano-remensis/sopor.texto: Manuscript of 50 leaves (National Library of France)

fuentes/codice-telleriano-remensis/resum.texto: Colonial codex in three parts: the calendar of festivals, the divinatory calendar, and annals running from the Mexica migration to 1562. The annals record the dedication of the Templo Mayor in 1487, wars, eclipses, the arrival of the Spaniards and colonial events, with glosses by several hands, among them that of the Dominican Pedro de los Ríos.

fuentes/codice-telleriano-remensis/por_q.texto: It is one of the most complete pictographic sources on the Mexica calendar and chronology.

fuentes/carta-del-cabildo-de-veracruz/ti.texto: Letter from the Cabildo of the Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz

fuentes/carta-del-cabildo-de-veracruz/au.texto: Cabildo of the Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz

fuentes/carta-del-cabildo-de-veracruz/re.texto: Letter dated July 10, 1519, from the council of the town that Cortés's men had just founded, addressed to Queen Juana and Charles V. It recounts the expeditions of Hernández de Córdoba and Grijalva and Cortés's expedition up to the founding of Veracruz, asks that the authority of Diego Velázquez be disregarded, and describes the human sacrifices the Spaniards say they saw, presented as a reason for the conquest.

fuentes/carta-del-cabildo-de-veracruz/po.texto: It usually stands in for Cortés's first letter, which is lost, and it is the first document through which the expedition sought legitimacy before the Crown.

fuentes/historia-verdadera-bernal/titulo.texto: The True History of the Conquest of New Spain

fuentes/historia-verdadera-bernal/soport.texto: Manuscripts from Guatemala and Madrid; published in Madrid in 1632

fuentes/historia-verdadera-bernal/resume.texto: Memoirs of a soldier of the expeditions of 1517, 1518 and 1519, who recounts the conquest of Mexico day by day, with the names of companions, horses and Indigenous captains: the admiration before Tenochtitlan and its market, the battles with the Tlaxcalans, the massacre at Cholula, the capture of Moctezuma, La Noche Triste and the siege. He describes temples stained with blood, sacrifices and the ritual consumption of human flesh, and also the branding and the distribution of Indigenous slaves among the conquistadors. He wrote it decades later, from memory and to claim rewards for the soldiers.

fuentes/historia-verdadera-bernal/por_qu.texto: It is the most widely read account of the conquest, with a voice close to the events, although sometimes mistaken about dates and figures and written against Gómara's version.

fuentes/historia-verdadera-bernal/leer.0.texto: Spanish edition at Project Gutenberg (volume 1 of 3)

fuentes/historia-verdadera-bernal/leer.1.texto: English translation by John Ingram Lockhart (1844), volume 1, at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/historia-de-la-conquista-gomara/.texto: Conquest of Mexico (second part of the General History of the Indies)

Biography of Cortés and account of the conquest written by his chaplain with the information that Cortés and others gave him, without having been to America. It describes the customs and religion of the Mexica, with sacrifices and cannibalism, and recounts the conquest as the work of Cortés's skill and courage. In 1553 a royal decree ordered the book withdrawn, for reasons not known with certainty, but it kept circulating and was translated into Italian, French and English.
It was the most widely disseminated version of the conquest in Europe in the 16th century, and it provoked Bernal Díaz's response.
English translation by Thomas Nicholas (1578) at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/relacion-de-andres-de-tapia/titu.texto: Account of Some of the Things That Happened to the Most Illustrious Lord Don Hernando Cortés

fuentes/relacion-de-andres-de-tapia/resu.texto: Account by one of Cortés's captains from the departure from Cuba to Narváez's defeat in 1520. It describes the great temple of Tenochtitlan and the rack of skulls in front of it, whose number he estimates at 136,000, and recounts how Cortés struck the temple's images with an iron bar. Gómara used it, and it was published only in the 19th century.

fuentes/relacion-de-andres-de-tapia/por_.texto: It is one of the few direct Spanish testimonies from someone who saw the sacred precinct before its destruction; the archaeology of the Huey Tzompantli confirmed the type of structure he describes, though not his figure.

fuentes/relacion-breve-de-francisco-de-a.texto: Brief Account of the Conquest of New Spain

Brief memoir of an old soldier of Cortés, dictated when he was already a Dominican friar and very elderly. It recounts the march to Tenochtitlan, the capture of Moctezuma, La Noche Triste and the siege, and describes the temples, the sacrifices and the skulls, with scenes of violence from both sides.
It is the late view of a direct participant, useful for contrasting with Cortés and Bernal Díaz.

fuentes/residencia-de-pedro-de-alvarado/.texto: Residencia Proceedings against Pedro de Alvarado
Published in Mexico in 1847 by José Fernando Ramírez

Residencia trial opened in 1529 against Alvarado, with the charges and the witness statements about his conduct in Mexico and in Guatemala. Among the charges is the massacre at the Toxcatl festival of 1520, which the witnesses describe as an attack on Mexica nobles who were dancing in the temple courtyard; Alvarado replied that they were preparing an uprising.
It is the main judicial document on the massacre at the Templo Mayor, and it shows that the conduct of the conquistadors was judged in their own time, although Alvarado was not punished for it.
1847 edition by José Fernando Ramírez on the Internet Archive

fuentes/juicio-de-residencia-de-cortes/a.texto: First Audiencia of Mexico and Council of the Indies

fuentes/juicio-de-residencia-de-cortes/r.texto: Proceedings opened in 1529 by the first Audiencia of Mexico, presided over by Nuño de Guzmán, an enemy of Cortés. Witnesses accused him, among other things, of the massacre at Cholula, of allowing the torture of Cuauhtémoc and the lord of Tacuba to obtain gold, and of keeping part of the booty; Cortés presented his own witnesses. The case dragged on for years in the Council of the Indies without a sentence.

fuentes/juicio-de-residencia-de-cortes/p.texto: It brings together dozens of conquistador testimonies on disputed events of the conquest, although many witnesses had interests for or against Cortés.

fuentes/proceso-contra-el-cazonci/titulo.texto: Trial of Tzintzicha Tangaxoan, the Cazonci

fuentes/proceso-contra-el-cazonci/soport.texto: Archivo General de Indias; published in 1952 by France V. Scholes and Eleanor B. Adams

fuentes/proceso-contra-el-cazonci/resume.texto: Record of the summary trial that Nuño de Guzmán conducted against the last Purépecha cazonci in February 1530, during his march to the west. It contains the charges of idolatry, of having killed Spaniards and of preparing an ambush, the statements obtained under torture from the cazonci and his associates, and the death sentence.

fuentes/proceso-contra-el-cazonci/por_qu.texto: It documents, in the words of its authors, how torture and a formal trial were used to strip and eliminate an Indigenous ruler who had submitted peacefully.

fuentes/codice-de-huexotzinco/idioma_ori.texto: Nahua pictography with glosses in Spanish

fuentes/codice-de-huexotzinco/soporte.texto: Eight sheets of amate paper (Library of Congress, United States)

fuentes/codice-de-huexotzinco/resumen.texto: Paintings presented as evidence in the lawsuit that Hernán Cortés brought in 1531 against the judges of the first Audiencia, including Nuño de Guzmán. They record the tribute the Huexotzincas had to deliver to the Audiencia in mantles, food, gold, labor and men for the expedition to Nueva Galicia, and a banner of the Virgin made of gold and feathers that was also demanded of them.

fuentes/codice-de-huexotzinco/por_que_im.texto: It shows that Indigenous peoples used their own records as evidence in Spanish courts to denounce abuses.

fuentes/relacion-de-acazitli/titulo.texto: Account of the Campaign Undertaken by Don Francisco de Sandoval Acazitli

fuentes/relacion-de-acazitli/resumen.texto: Account of the participation of the lord of Tlalmanalco, Francisco de Sandoval Acazitli, and his warriors in the campaign of Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza against the Caxcanes during the Mixtón War. It narrates the marches, the sieges of the hilltop strongholds, the booty and the captives, and shows Nahua nobles fighting as allies of the Crown.

fuentes/relacion-de-acazitli/por_que_imp.texto: It is a rare testimony from an Indigenous ally about a conquest campaign, and it shows that the Mixtón War was fought largely by Indigenous warriors from central Mexico.

fuentes/historia-de-yucatan-cogolludo/re.texto: Franciscan chronicle of Yucatán from the voyages of Hernández de Córdoba and Grijalva to the middle of the 17th century: the campaigns of the Montejo family, the founding of Mérida, evangelization, conflicts among friars, encomenderos and governors, and Maya rebellions. It reproduces documents now lost and defends the work of his order.

fuentes/historia-de-yucatan-cogolludo/po.texto: It is the main chronicle of the conquest of Yucatán and one of the foundations of colonial Maya history.

fuentes/historia-de-yucatan-cogolludo/le.texto: Historia de Yucathan, original 1688 edition, on the Internet Archive

fuentes/historia-de-la-conquista-del-itz.texto: History of the Conquest of the Province of El Itzá

Official history, written in Madrid by an official of the Council of the Indies using the case files, of the conquest of the Itzás of Petén: Cortés's visit in 1525, the Franciscan entries of the 17th century, the road opened by Martín de Ursúa from Yucatán, and the assault on Nojpetén in 1697. It justifies the conquest by evangelization and by the Itzás' refusal to submit.
Together with the Archivo de Indias files, it is the main source on the fall of the last independent Maya kingdom.
Original 1701 edition on the Internet Archive

fuentes/historia-de-la-conquista-de-mexi.texto: History of the Conquest of Mexico, Population and Progress of North America

Narrative of the conquest up to the fall of Tenochtitlan, based on Cortés, Gómara, Bernal Díaz and Antonio de Herrera, and written as a literary work by the chief chronicler of the Indies. It presents the conquest as a providential enterprise to end idolatry and sacrifice, with Cortés as hero.
It was the most widely read version of the conquest in Europe for more than a century, and an early example of the apologetic view.

fuentes/history-of-the-conquest-of-mexic.texto: History of the Conquest of Mexico

Three-volume history based on copies of documents from Spanish archives, which the author had gathered, though he never traveled to Mexico. It describes Mexica civilization with admiration and with horror at its sacrifices, and narrates the conquest as a drama between Cortés and Moctezuma in which the Indigenous allies have little place.
For a century it was the standard reference work in English and shaped the popular image of the conquest; its account, centered on the Spaniards and on European superiority, is now widely disputed.

fuentes/aztec-warfare/titulo.texto: Aztec Warfare: Imperial Expansion and Political Control

fuentes/aztec-warfare/resumen.texto: Study of the Triple Alliance's warfare: recruitment, training, weapons, logistics and marching routes, and their relation to tribute. It argues that Mexica dominance was hegemonic and indirect, leaving subjected rulers in power in exchange for tribute, and it discusses the figures for sacrifice victims and the role of the flower wars.

fuentes/aztec-warfare/por_que_importa.texto: It is the standard reference on Mexica warfare and helps explain why so many subjected peoples allied with the Spaniards.

fuentes/mexico-and-the-spanish-conquest/.texto: Military history of the conquest explained from the perspective of Indigenous politics: the Spaniards contributed steel weapons, horses and brigantines, but the war was decided by tens of thousands of warriors from Tlaxcala, Texcoco, Chalco and other peoples, who seized the chance to free themselves from Mexica rule or to gain ground against their rivals.
It is one of the works that shifted the story of the conquest toward the role of Indigenous allies.

fuentes/la-conquista-de-mexico-thomas/re.texto: Detailed narrative of the conquest, from the Castilian and Antillean context to the fall of Tenochtitlan and its consequences, based on extensive use of archival documents, residencia trials and probanzas. It attends both to Mexica society and to the conquistadors and their internal disputes.

fuentes/la-conquista-de-mexico-thomas/po.texto: It is the most complete narrative synthesis of the conquest written at the end of the 20th century.

fuentes/aztecs-clendinnen/resumen.texto: Study of the society of Tenochtitlan on the eve of the conquest, drawing above all on the Florentine Codex: war, sacrifice, festivals, and the lives of warriors, women and merchants. It seeks to understand human sacrifice from the perspective of religion and of the Mexica's own experience, without reducing it to Spanish propaganda or to a material necessity.

fuentes/aztecs-clendinnen/por_que_import.texto: It is one of the most influential interpretations of Mexica ritual violence.

fuentes/when-montezuma-met-cortes/resume.texto: Re-examination of the meeting of November 8, 1519, and of the whole conquest. It argues that the speech in which Moctezuma supposedly handed his kingdom to Cortés is a construction by Cortés to present the conquest as lawful, that the idea that the Mexica took the Spaniards for gods is later, and that Moctezuma may have received them in order to keep them under control. It proposes speaking of a “Hispano-Aztec war.”

fuentes/when-montezuma-met-cortes/por_qu.texto: It is the main recent critique of the account inherited from Cortés, Sahagún and Prescott; its theses about Moctezuma's intentions are debated interpretations.

fuentes/malintzins-choices/resumen.texto: Biography of Malintzin reconstructed from Spanish and Nahua sources: her sale as a girl, her role as interpreter and negotiator, her son with Cortés, her marriage, her early death and the fate of her children. It interprets her decisions as those of an enslaved woman who owed no loyalty to the Mexica.

fuentes/malintzins-choices/por_que_impor.texto: It reviews, with documents, both the nationalist reading of La Malinche as a traitor and her idealization.

fuentes/fifth-sun/titulo.texto: Fifth Sun: A New History of the Aztecs

fuentes/fifth-sun/resumen.texto: History of the Mexica from the migration to the early 17th century, based on the annals written in Nahuatl after the conquest, such as those of Chimalpahin, Tezozómoc or Tlatelolco, rather than on Spanish chronicles. It treats sacrifice, war and slavery as part of Mexica politics, and follows the Nahua nobility in the colonial period.

fuentes/fifth-sun/por_que_importa.texto: It shows what the Nahua sources say about their own history when they are read in their language.

fuentes/burying-the-white-gods/titulo.texto: Burying the White Gods: New Perspectives on the Conquest of Mexico

fuentes/burying-the-white-gods/resumen.texto: Article that traces the origin of the idea that the Mexica believed the Spaniards were gods and that Cortés was Quetzalcoatl: it does not appear in Cortés's letters or in the earliest Nahua texts, but in written sources decades later. It explains the use of the word teotl for the Spaniards and argues that the Nahuas acted for political reasons, not out of confusion.

fuentes/burying-the-white-gods/por_que_i.texto: It is the most cited scholarly critique of the myth of the “white gods.”

fuentes/indian-conquistadors/titulo.texto: Indian Conquistadors: Indigenous Allies in the Conquest of Mesoamerica

fuentes/indian-conquistadors/autor.texto: Laura E. Matthew and Michel R. Oudijk (editors)

fuentes/indian-conquistadors/resumen.texto: Collected volume with studies of the Nahua, Zapotec, Mixtec and other warriors who accompanied the Spaniards in the conquest of Mexico, Guatemala, the west and the north, based on probanzas, painted cloths and lawsuits in which they themselves claimed rewards.

fuentes/indian-conquistadors/por_que_imp.texto: It showed that the conquest of Mesoamerica was largely the work of Indigenous armies with their own interests, and not only of a few hundred Spaniards.

fuentes/vision-de-los-vencidos/titulo.texto: The Broken Spears: Indigenous Accounts of the Conquest

fuentes/vision-de-los-vencidos/resumen.texto: Anthology of Nahua texts on the conquest, translated mainly by Ángel María Garibay: Book XII of the Florentine Codex, the Annals of Tlatelolco, laments and fragments of Tezozómoc, Muñoz Camargo and others. It presents the conquest from the point of view of the peoples of the Valley of Mexico.

fuentes/vision-de-los-vencidos/por_que_i.texto: It spread the Indigenous version of the conquest around the world and was translated into dozens of languages; later historians, such as James Lockhart, pointed out that it brings together under a single “voice of the vanquished” texts from different peoples, dates and interests, some from peoples allied with the Spaniards.

fuentes/sacrificio-humano-lopez-lujan-ol.texto: Human Sacrifice in the Mesoamerican Religious Tradition

Collective book coordinated by Leonardo López Luján and Guilhem Olivier, published by the INAH and UNAM, which brings together archaeological, osteological and historical studies of human sacrifice in Mesoamerica, from the Olmecs to the Mexica: the techniques, the victims, the treatment of the bodies and their religious meaning.
It summarizes what archaeology and the sources allow one to affirm about sacrifice, against those who denied it as Spanish propaganda and those who explained it solely by material needs.

fuentes/wade-2018-huey-tzompantli/titulo.texto: Feeding the Gods: Hundreds of Skulls Reveal the Scale of Human Sacrifice in the Aztec Capital

fuentes/wade-2018-huey-tzompantli/resume.texto: Article in Science on the excavations of the Huey Tzompantli of Tenochtitlan, carried out since 2015 by the INAH's Urban Archaeology Program, directed by Raúl Barrera. It describes the tower of skulls joined with lime and the platform of the rack, reports that the skulls studied were mostly young men but also women and children, and presents the archaeologists' interpretations of who the victims were.

fuentes/wade-2018-huey-tzompantli/por_qu.texto: It publicized data from one of the discoveries that confirmed, with physical evidence, the scale of sacrifice described by the chroniclers.

fuentes/tlaxcala-in-the-sixteenth-centur.texto: Study of Tlaxcala from the alliance with Cortés to the end of the 16th century: the privileges it obtained from the Crown, its Indigenous cabildo, evangelization, tribute, the decline of the population, and the Tlaxcalan families sent to settle the north in 1591.
It showed that the allies of the conquest obtained exceptional treatment, but did not escape the epidemics or the burdens of the colonial regime.

fuentes/conquest-of-michoacan-warren/res.texto: Documentary history of the subjugation of the Purépecha kingdom: the peaceful surrender of the cazonci in 1522, the encomiendas, Franciscan evangelization, and the trial and execution of the cazonci by Nuño de Guzmán in 1530.

fuentes/conquest-of-michoacan-warren/por.texto: It is the standard study of the conquest of Michoacán, based on judicial records.

fuentes/war-for-mexicos-west/resumen.texto: Study of the conquest of New Galicia and the Mixtón War: Nuño de Guzmán's expedition, the enslavement of captives, the encomiendas, the revolt of the Caxcanes and other peoples, and Viceroy Mendoza's campaign with tens of thousands of Indigenous allies.

fuentes/war-for-mexicos-west/por_que_imp.texto: It is the main modern monograph on the Mixtón War and on the violence of the conquest of the west.

fuentes/conquest-of-yucatan-chamberlain/.texto: The Conquest and Colonization of Yucatan, 1517–1550

History of the Montejo campaigns based on documents from the Archivo de Indias: the failures of 1527–1535, the division of the Maya lordships, the alliance with the Xiu of Maní, the founding of Mérida and the great rebellion of 1546–1547.
It is the classic study of the conquest of Yucatán, published by the Carnegie Institution of Washington.

fuentes/spanish-conquest-of-yucatan-mean.texto: History of the Spanish Conquest of Yucatan and of the Itzas
Papers of the Peabody Museum, Harvard University

Early study of the conquest of Yucatán and Petén, focused on the Franciscan entries of the 17th century and on Martín de Ursúa's conquest of the Itzás, with translations of passages by Villagutierre and other chroniclers.
It was the first academic study in English of the fall of the Itzás, and it is in the public domain.

fuentes/conquest-of-the-last-maya-kingdo.texto: The Conquest of the Last Maya Kingdom

Reconstruction, using Spanish documents and Maya testimony, of the Itzá kingdom of Nojpetén, its political organization and its fall: the negotiations of Ajaw Kan Ek', the division among Itzá factions, Martín de Ursúa's assault in 1697, and the epidemics and dispersal that followed.
It is the standard study of the Itzás and of the end of Maya independence.

personas/acamapichtli/resumen.texto: First tlatoani of Tenochtitlan according to Mexica chronicles, of Culhua lineage, elected around 1375. In his time the Mexica were tributaries of the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco and fought as their allies.

personas/itzcoatl/resumen.texto: Fourth tlatoani of Tenochtitlan (1427–1440). With Nezahualcóyotl of Texcoco he defeated Azcapotzalco in 1428 and formed the Triple Alliance with Tlacopan. According to Sahagún's informants, the old historical paintings were burned in his time, which many historians read as an official rewriting of the Mexica past.

personas/moctezuma-i/resumen.texto: Fifth tlatoani of Tenochtitlan (1440–1469). He extended the domination of the Triple Alliance toward the Gulf coast and Oaxaca, and governed during the great famine of 1450–1454; Durán places in his time the pact of the flower wars with Tlaxcala and Huexotzinco.

personas/axayacatl/resumen.texto: Sixth tlatoani (1469–1481) and father of Moctezuma II. In 1473 he conquered Tlatelolco, the twin city of Tenochtitlan, whose ruler Moquíhuix died in the fighting; around 1479 he suffered, at the hands of the Purépecha, the greatest Mexica defeat known before 1519.

personas/tizoc/resumen.texto: Seventh tlatoani (1481–1486), with a brief reign and few conquests. Some sources say he died poisoned by nobles of his court. The Tízoc Stone, a large monolith carved with scenes of the capture of warriors from other peoples, bears his name.

personas/ahuitzotl/resumen.texto: Eighth tlatoani (1486–1502). He carried the campaigns of the Triple Alliance as far as Soconusco, on the Pacific coast, and in 1487 dedicated the enlargement of the Templo Mayor with a mass sacrifice of prisoners whose number is debated. An aqueduct he had brought from Coyoacán flooded the city around 1500.

personas/tlacaelel/resumen.texto: Cihuacóatl, the chief counselor of several tlatoque of Tenochtitlan from Itzcóatl onward. The chronicles of Durán and Tezozómoc, which follow the same lost Nahua source, attribute to him the religious reform that put Huitzilopochtli at the center, the drive for expansion and the flower wars; the Texcocan sources hardly mention him, and several historians suspect that this common source enlarged his role.

personas/cuitlahuac/resumen.texto: Brother of Moctezuma II and lord of Iztapalapa. Held by the Spaniards and released in 1520, he led the attack that drove them out of the city on La Noche Triste, and he was elected tlatoani; he died of smallpox at the end of 1520, about eighty days later.

personas/cuauhtemoc/resumen.texto: Last tlatoani of Tenochtitlan (1520–1521), son of Ahuízotl and cousin of Moctezuma II. He directed the defense of the city during the siege and was captured on August 13, 1521. The Spaniards burned his feet to make him say where the gold was; Cortés took him as a hostage on his expedition to Honduras and had him hanged in 1525, accused of conspiracy.

personas/isabel-moctezuma/resumen.texto: Daughter of Moctezuma II, married successively to Cuitláhuac and to Cuauhtémoc. After the conquest she was baptized, had a daughter with Cortés and married three Spaniards; in 1526 Cortés granted her the encomienda of Tacuba, one of the largest in the Valley of Mexico, which her descendants defended in lawsuits for generations.

personas/tetlepanquetzal/resumen.texto: Tlatoani of Tlacopan, the third city of the Triple Alliance, during the siege of Tenochtitlan. He was tortured together with Cuauhtémoc to make him reveal where the gold was, and he was hanged with him in 1525.

personas/nezahualcoyotl/resumen.texto: Tlatoani of Texcoco (1431–1472). As a young man he saw his father killed by the Tepanecs and lived in exile; allied with the Mexica, he defeated Azcapotzalco in 1428 and formed the Triple Alliance, with which Texcoco shared the wars of conquest, the tribute and the sacrifice of captives. Laws, hydraulic works such as the albarradón (dike) of 1449, and poems in the Cantares mexicanos are attributed to him; his image as a wise king owes much to his descendant Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxóchitl.

personas/nezahualpilli/resumen.texto: Tlatoani of Texcoco (1472–1515) and son of Nezahualcóyotl. Texcocan sources present him as an astrologer and a stern lawgiver, who had one of his wives, a daughter of Axayácatl, executed for adultery. At his death the succession was disputed between Cacamatzin, backed by Moctezuma II, and Ixtlilxóchitl, which divided Texcoco before the arrival of the Spaniards.

personas/cacamatzin/resumen.texto: Tlatoani of Texcoco from 1516 and nephew of Moctezuma II. He accompanied his uncle when they received Cortés; accused of preparing a revolt, he was handed over to the Spaniards and held prisoner along with Moctezuma. He died in 1520, in the days of La Noche Triste, in circumstances that the sources describe in different ways.

personas/ixtlilxochitl-ii/resumen.texto: Son of Nezahualpilli who disputed the throne of Texcoco with his brother Cacamatzin. He allied with Cortés, was baptized as Fernando, and brought thousands of Texcocan warriors to the siege of Tenochtitlan. His descendant Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxóchitl gave him a decisive role in the conquest in his works, a role other sources do not grant him to that extent.

personas/xicotencatl-el-viejo/resumen.texto: Lord of Tizatlán, one of the four cabeceras of Tlaxcala, already very old in 1519. He was one of the Tlaxcalan lords who, after the battles of September 1519, accepted the alliance with Cortés against the Mexica.

personas/maxixcatzin/resumen.texto: Lord of Ocotelulco, another of the four cabeceras of Tlaxcala, and the main defender of the alliance with the Spaniards; after La Noche Triste he received them in Tlaxcala and upheld the alliance against those who wanted to break it. He died of smallpox at the end of 1520.

personas/xicotencatl-el-joven/resumen.texto: Tlaxcalan captain, son of Xicohténcatl the Elder, who led the fighting against Cortés in September 1519 and distrusted the alliance. During the preparations for the siege of Tenochtitlan he left the army, and Cortés had him hanged in 1521. Nineteenth-century Mexican nationalism made him a symbol of opposition to the Spaniards.

personas/tangaxoan-ii/resumen.texto: Last irecha, or cazonci, of the Purépecha kingdom, with its capital at Tzintzuntzan. In 1522 he submitted to the Spaniards without war and was baptized as Francisco; in 1530 Nuño de Guzmán had him tortured to obtain gold, tried him for conspiracy, and had him executed and burned. The trial brought against him survives.

personas/francisco-tenamaztle/resumen.texto: Caxcan lord of Nochistlán and one of the leaders of the Mixtón War (1540–1542). He kept fighting until he surrendered around 1551; deported to Spain, he presented in 1555, with help from Las Casas, a petition to the Council of the Indies that justified the rebellion by the abuses of encomenderos and conquistadors.

personas/ajaw-kan-ek/resumen.texto: King of the Itzás, the last independent Maya kingdom, with its capital at Nojpetén, on Lake Petén Itzá. Between 1695 and 1696 he received embassies and Franciscan missionaries and negotiated a submission that was never carried out; he was captured in Martín de Ursúa's assault of March 13, 1697, and taken prisoner to Santiago de Guatemala.

personas/malinche/resumen.texto: Nahua woman from the Gulf coast, given as a girl to the Chontal Maya of Tabasco, who gave her to Cortés with nineteen other women after the battle of Centla (1519). She spoke Nahuatl and Maya and was Cortés's interpreter throughout the conquest; she had a son with him, Martín, and in 1524 she married Juan Jaramillo. The Tlaxcalan codices show her at the center of the negotiations; nineteenth-century nationalism made her a symbol of treason, and recent studies, such as Camilla Townsend's, analyze her decisions in their context.

personas/jeronimo-de-aguilar/resumen.texto: Spanish priest who was shipwrecked in Yucatán in 1511 and lived eight years as a captive among the Maya. In 1519 he joined Cortés at Cozumel and translated from Maya; together with Malintzin, who went from Nahuatl to Maya, he formed the chain of translation of the conquest's first months.

personas/gonzalo-guerrero/resumen.texto: Sailor from the same 1511 shipwreck who, according to Bernal Díaz, integrated into Maya society at Chetumal, married a noblewoman, had children and refused to return to the Spaniards. Spanish sources accuse him of leading Maya resistance against the Montejos and say that he died in 1536 in Honduras, fighting alongside Indigenous people.

personas/francisco-hernandez-de-cordoba-.texto: Cuban settler who in 1517 led the first Spanish expedition to Yucatán: according to Bernal Díaz, to discover new lands; according to Las Casas, to capture Indians as slaves. He saw stone Maya cities at Cape Catoche and Campeche, was defeated at Champotón, and died of his wounds on the way back to Cuba. He is not the founder of the Nicaraguan cities of the same name.

personas/juan-de-grijalva/resumen.texto: Relative of Diego Velázquez who in 1518 led the second expedition to Yucatán and the Gulf coast: he explored Cozumel, Tabasco and Veracruz, where envoys of Moctezuma exchanged gifts with him. The news of gold he brought back led to Cortés's expedition. He died in 1527 in Central America, in an Indigenous attack.

personas/pedro-de-alvarado/resumen.texto: Conquistador from Extremadura and Cortés's lieutenant. He was left in charge of the Spaniards in Tenochtitlan in May 1520 and directed the massacre at the Toxcatl festival, one of the charges in his residencia trial of 1529. From 1524 he led the conquest of Guatemala; he died in 1541, days after a horse fell on him during the assault on the hilltop stronghold of Nochistlán, in the Mixtón War.

personas/panfilo-de-narvaez/resumen.texto: Conquistador of Cuba, where Las Casas accused him of allowing the massacre at Caonao (1513). Diego Velázquez sent him in 1520 with some 800 to 900 men to arrest Cortés, who defeated him at Cempoala and added his soldiers to his own; the chronicles attribute the spread of smallpox to an enslaved African in his fleet. He died in 1528 in the shipwreck of his expedition to Florida.

personas/gonzalo-de-sandoval/resumen.texto: Conquistador from Extremadura and one of Cortés's most trusted captains: he commanded troops at the siege of Tenochtitlan and in the campaigns of the Gulf coast, where he founded Espíritu Santo, in Coatzacoalcos. He died in 1528 at Palos, while returning to Spain with Cortés.

personas/cristobal-de-olid/resumen.texto: Captain of Cortés at the siege of Tenochtitlan and in the 1522 entry into Michoacán. Sent to Honduras in 1524, he rebelled against Cortés in agreement with Diego Velázquez and was killed that same year by other Spaniards; his rebellion prompted Cortés's expedition to the Hibueras.

personas/andres-de-tapia/resumen.texto: Soldier and captain of Cortés who wrote an account of the conquest up to Narváez's defeat (1520), used by Gómara. He described the great temple and its tzompantli, and stated that he and another soldier counted 136,000 skulls there, a figure that could not be verified.

personas/francisco-de-aguilar/resumen.texto: Soldier of Cortés named Alonso de Aguilar, who years later gave up his property and became a Dominican under the name Francisco. Already very old, he dictated, at the request of his brothers in the order, a Brief Account of the Conquest of New Spain that describes Mexica rites and the violence of both sides.

personas/bernal-diaz-del-castillo/resume.texto: Soldier in the expeditions of Hernández de Córdoba, Grijalva and Cortés. In old age, as an encomendero in Santiago de Guatemala, he wrote The True History of the Conquest of New Spain, partly to correct Gómara and to claim credit for the common soldiers; it was published in 1632.

personas/nuno-de-guzman/resumen.texto: Castilian lawyer, appointed governor of Pánuco in 1525, where he had thousands of enslaved Indians sold to the Antilles, and president of the first Audiencia of Mexico (1528–1530), which Bishop Zumárraga denounced. Between 1529 and 1531 he conquered the west, which he named New Galicia, with massacres, burned towns and the enslavement of captives; earlier he had had the cazonci of Michoacán executed. He was arrested in 1537 and died in Spain without recovering his offices.

personas/francisco-de-montejo/resumen.texto: Conquistador from Salamanca who took part in the expeditions of Grijalva and Cortés and in 1526 obtained from the king the capitulation to conquer Yucatán. His campaigns of 1527–1535 failed against the Maya lordships; the conquest was completed between 1540 and 1546 by his son and nephew, both named Francisco. He lost his governorships in a residencia trial and died in Spain.

personas/francisco-de-montejo-el-mozo/re.texto: Son of the adelantado of the same name. He led the 1540–1542 campaign in Yucatán, allied with the Xiu lordship of Maní, founded Campeche, and on January 6, 1542 founded Mérida over the Maya city of T'ho.

personas/martin-de-ursua/resumen.texto: Navarrese military officer and governor of Yucatán, who opened a road from Mérida toward Petén and on March 13, 1697 took Nojpetén, the Itzás' capital, by assault. He later became governor of the Philippines, where he died.

personas/francisco-lopez-de-gomara/resum.texto: Castilian humanist cleric, Cortés's chaplain in Spain, who never went to America. His General History of the Indies (1552), whose second part is the Conquest of Mexico, was based on Cortés's papers and accounts and presents him as almost the sole protagonist; in 1553 an order was issued to recall it, and Bernal Díaz wrote in part to refute it.

personas/diego-duran/resumen.texto: Dominican born in Seville and raised in Texcoco and Mexico City, who spoke Nahuatl. He wrote the History of the Indies of New Spain (finished around 1581), based on a lost Nahua chronicle, on paintings and on informants, with the stated aim that the friars would recognize the ancient rites in order to eradicate them. It is the source of the figure of 80,400 sacrificed in 1487.

personas/juan-de-tovar/resumen.texto: Novohispanic Jesuit who spoke Nahuatl and who around 1585 wrote an illustrated account of the origin and rites of the Mexica, related to Durán's work. José de Acosta used it in his Natural and Moral History of the Indies (1590).

personas/hernando-alvarado-tezozomoc/res.texto: Nahua noble, grandson of Moctezuma II through his mother, and interpreter for the Royal Audiencia. He wrote in Spanish the Crónica mexicana (around 1598), on the history of Tenochtitlan up to Cortés's arrival, and he is credited with the Crónica mexicáyotl (1609), in Nahuatl, which we know through Chimalpahin's copy.

personas/diego-munoz-camargo/resumen.texto: Mestizo, son of a conquistador and a Nahua woman, interpreter and influential resident of Tlaxcala. He wrote the Description of the City and Province of Tlaxcala (around 1580–1585), for the questionnaire of the relaciones geográficas, and a History of Tlaxcala; both defend the services of the Tlaxcalans to the Crown.

personas/juan-bautista-pomar/resumen.texto: Mestizo of Texcoco, great-grandson of Nezahualcóyotl on his mother's side, who in 1582 wrote the Relación de Texcoco for the questionnaire of the relaciones geográficas, with information on the government, religion and sacrifices of the ancient Texcocans.

personas/fernando-de-alva-ixtlilxochitl/.texto: Mestizo historian, descendant of the tlatoque of Texcoco, who was Indigenous governor of Texcoco and Tlalmanalco and interpreter for the Juzgado General de Indios. He wrote in Spanish, using codices and Texcocan testimony, several relaciones and the History of the Chichimec Nation, which exalt Nezahualcóyotl and his ancestor Ixtlilxóchitl II as Cortés's ally.

personas/chimalpahin/nombre.texto: Chimalpahin (Domingo Francisco de San Antón Muñón Chimalpahin Cuauhtlehuanitzin)

personas/chimalpahin/resumen.texto: Nahua historian born in Amecameca, who lived as a lay servant (donado) of the church of San Antonio Abad in Mexico City. He wrote in Nahuatl, using codices and accounts from his region, several relaciones focused on the lordships of Chalco and Amecameca and a diary of his time, and he copied and annotated the Crónica mexicáyotl.

personas/antonio-de-solis/resumen.texto: Playwright and chief chronicler of the Indies, who published in 1684 the History of the Conquest of Mexico, an elegant and apologetic account of Cortés that was the most widely read account of the conquest in Europe until Prescott.

personas/diego-lopez-de-cogolludo/resume.texto: Franciscan from Alcalá de Henares who lived in Yucatán from 1634 and wrote the Historia de Yucathan (1688), the principal chronicle of the conquest and evangelization of the peninsula, with documents now lost.

personas/ross-hassig/resumen.texto: American anthropologist and historian (1945–2025), a specialist in Mexica warfare. In Aztec Warfare (1988) and Mexico and the Spanish Conquest (1994) he studied the logistics, military organization and tribute of the Triple Alliance, and argued that the conquest was above all a war of Indigenous allies against Tenochtitlan.

personas/hugh-thomas/resumen.texto: British historian, author of The Conquest of Mexico (1993), an extensive narrative based on archival documents that had been little used until then, such as residencia trials and the probanzas of the conquistadors.

personas/camilla-townsend/resumen.texto: American historian of the Nahua peoples who works with the Nahuatl annals. She wrote about the figure of Malintzin (2006) and a history of the Mexica based on their own sources, Fifth Sun (2019), and she criticized the idea that the Mexica took the Spaniards for gods.

personas/leonardo-lopez-lujan/resumen.texto: Mexican archaeologist, director since 1991 of the Templo Mayor Project of the INAH. He studied the offerings of the sacred precinct of Tenochtitlan, among them human sacrifice remains, and with Guilhem Olivier coordinated in 2010 a reference book on sacrifice in Mesoamerica.

personas/eduardo-matos-moctezuma/resumen.texto: Mexican archaeologist who from 1978 directed the excavation of the Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan, begun after the discovery of the Coyolxauhqui stone, and was the first director of its museum.

personas/alfredo-lopez-austin/resumen.texto: Mexican historian of Mesoamerican religion and worldview, author of Cuerpo humano e ideología (1980), which studied ideas about the body, sacrifice and the gods from Nahuatl-language sources.

hechos/pueblo-mexica/resumen.texto: Nahuatl-speaking people who, according to their tradition, arrived in the Valley of Mexico from a northern place called Aztlán and founded Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco on islets in Lake Texcoco. In less than a century, from 1428, they went from being tributaries of the Tepanecs to heading the Triple Alliance, which collected tribute from much of Mesoamerica. They built one of the largest cities of their time, with chinampas, aqueducts, schools and markets, and practiced wars of conquest, mass human sacrifice and slavery; after 1521 their nobility kept offices and lands for a time under Spanish rule, and their language continued to be written for centuries with the Latin alphabet that the friars taught.

hechos/pueblo-tlaxcalteca/resumen.texto: Nahuatl-speaking people, with Otomí minorities, organized into a confederation of four lordships (Tizatlán, Ocotelulco, Quiahuiztlan and Tepeticpac) that governed by council. Surrounded by Triple Alliance territories, they kept their independence in permanent war with the Mexica, without access to the salt and cotton trade according to what they told the Spaniards. Like the Mexica, they sacrificed captives taken in those wars. In 1519 they allied with Cortés and were decisive in the conquest, which earned them privileges that they defended throughout the colonial period.

hechos/itzaes-del-peten/resumen.texto: Maya people who, according to their tradition, migrated from Yucatán to Lake Petén Itzá and founded there the kingdom of Nojpetén, ruled by a king of the Kan Ek' lineage together with a council of lords and priests. It kept its independence for nearly two centuries after the fall of Tenochtitlan, received Maya refugees from the conquered areas and rejected several Spanish missions; the Franciscans and Spaniards accused it of sacrificing missionaries and captives. Its kingdom fell in 1697.

hechos/migracion-mexica/resumen.texto: According to Mexica codices and chronicles, the Mexica left Aztlán guided by their god Huitzilopochtli and, after some two centuries of wandering, reached the Valley of Mexico, where they served as mercenaries and tributaries of older peoples such as Culhuacán and Azcapotzalco. The sources do not agree on the date of departure, Aztlán was never identified, and many historians consider it a mythical place; the account was reworked by the Mexica nobility itself after its rise.

hechos/triple-alianza-mexica/titulo.texto: The Triple Alliance: Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan

hechos/triple-alianza-mexica/resumen.texto: In 1428 Tenochtitlan, ruled by Itzcóatl, Texcoco under Nezahualcóyotl and Tlacopan defeated the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco, to whom they had paid tribute, and formed an alliance that for ninety years subjected much of central and southern Mexico to tribute. It was not an empire with governors everywhere: in general it left local lords in place in exchange for tribute and obedience, with garrisons and tax collectors at some points. Tenochtitlan gradually gained predominance over its two partners.

hechos/quema-de-pinturas-de-itzcoatl/tit.texto: The Burning of the Historical Paintings in the Time of Itzcóatl

hechos/quema-de-pinturas-de-itzcoatl/res.texto: Nahua informants of Sahagún recounted that, when Itzcóatl governed, Mexica lords ordered the ancient paintings burned, because it was not fitting for common people to know them and because they contained lies. Many historians interpret this as an official rewriting of Mexica history after the victory over Azcapotzalco; it is the only account of the event, and its extent is unknown.

hechos/conquista-de-chalco/titulo.texto: The War of Tenochtitlan against Chalco

hechos/conquista-de-chalco/resumen.texto: For about two decades the Triple Alliance fought the confederation of Chalco, southeast of the Valley of Mexico, until subjugating it around 1465, in the time of Moctezuma Ilhuicamina. Chimalpahin, born in Amecameca, recounts it from the Chalca side, with its defeats, the exile of its lords and the subsequent tribute. In 1521 the Chalcas joined the Spaniards against Tenochtitlan.

hechos/albarradon-de-nezahualcoyotl/resu.texto: After a great flood, Moctezuma Ilhuicamina asked Nezahualcóyotl for help, and he directed the construction of a dike of stone, earth and stakes some 16 kilometers long across the lake, from Atzacoalco to Iztapalapa, built with the labor of subject peoples. It separated the fresh waters surrounding Tenochtitlan from the brackish waters of Lake Texcoco and protected the city from floods.

hechos/gran-hambruna-de-1454/resumen.texto: Frosts, droughts and plagues ruined several harvests in a row in the Valley of Mexico in the time of Moctezuma Ilhuicamina. Chronicles say that many people died or emigrated and that many sold themselves as slaves, or sold their children, to the Totonacs of the coast in exchange for maize, until the good harvest of 1455. Some historians connect it with the pact of the Flower Wars, which Durán places in those years.

hechos/chinampas-del-valle-de-mexico/tit.texto: The Chinampas of the Valley of Mexico

hechos/chinampas-del-valle-de-mexico/res.texto: The Mexica and their neighbors in Xochimilco and Chalco farmed chinampas, plots reclaimed from the lake with layers of mud and aquatic plants, held in place with stakes and trees and watered by canals, which yielded several harvests a year of maize, beans, chili, squash and flowers. Together with tribute and the Tlatelolco market they supplied a city that archaeologists estimate at about 150,000 to more than 200,000 inhabitants. The chinampas of Xochimilco are still in use and have been a World Heritage Site since 1987.

hechos/educacion-mexica/resumen.texto: According to the Codex Mendoza and Sahagún's informants, all Mexica boys attended a school: the sons of nobles, and some commoners, attended the calmécac next to the temples, where they trained as priests, officials and leaders in pictographic writing, the calendar and songs; the rest attended the telpochcalli of their neighborhood, focused on war and collective labor. Girls were educated mainly at home and some in the temples. The Codex Mendoza also shows punishments for children, such as pricking them with maguey spines or exposing them to chili smoke.

hechos/tributo-de-la-triple-alianza/titu.texto: The Tribute of the Triple Alliance

hechos/tributo-de-la-triple-alianza/resu.texto: The Codex Mendoza and the Matrícula de tributos record what some 400 peoples grouped into 38 provinces handed over: tens of thousands of cotton mantles, warrior costumes, cacao, maize, beans, feathers, gold, paper and other products, every eighty days, every six months or every year, along with labor and warriors. Many subject peoples experienced it as a burden: Bernal Díaz recounts that the Totonacs of Cempoala complained to Cortés that Moctezuma's tax collectors were carrying off their sons and daughters to sacrifice them, and Chimalpahin recalls the subjugation of Chalco. Ross Hassig and other historians describe it as hegemonic domination, which explains why so many peoples allied with the Spaniards.

hechos/guerras-floridas/resumen.texto: According to Durán, Tezozómoc and Ixtlilxóchitl, the Triple Alliance maintained agreed, periodic wars with Tlaxcala, Huexotzinco and Cholula whose purpose was to capture warriors for sacrifice and to train young men, not to conquer; the sources place their origin in the mid-15th century and attribute it to Tlacaélel or Nezahualcóyotl. Ross Hassig and other historians hold that they also served to wear down enemies the Triple Alliance could not defeat at once. The Tlaxcalans, surrounded and, as they told the Spaniards, without access to salt and cotton, experienced them as a real war, and that enmity partly explains their alliance with Cortés.

hechos/sacrificio-humano-mexica/resumen.texto: Nahua and Spanish sources describe sacrifices at almost every festival of the calendar: mostly of war captives, but also of purchased slaves, women and children. The most common form was heart extraction on a stone, and there were also beheading, arrow-shooting and unequal combat on the gladiatorial stone. Archaeology of the Templo Mayor confirmed it with offerings containing remains of sacrificial victims, such as those of at least 42 children dedicated to Tlaloc in Offering 48, and with the Huey Tzompantli. For the Mexica it fed the gods who sustained the world; today the figures are debated, but not the existence of sacrifice, which some authors, such as the ethnologist Peter Hassler in the 1990s, went so far as to deny as a Spanish invention.

hechos/canibalismo-ritual-mexica/titulo.texto: The Ritual Consumption of Human Flesh

hechos/canibalismo-ritual-mexica/resumen.texto: Sahagún's informants, Durán, Bernal Díaz and others recount that, after certain sacrifices, the warrior who had captured the captive received his body and his family ate a portion in a ritual meal, while the captor did not taste the flesh of his own captive, whom he called son. Bernal Díaz further stated that in many peoples there were wooden cages where captives were fattened to be sacrificed and eaten. Human bones with cut and defleshing marks found at sites in central Mexico, among them Tecoaque, are consistent with those practices, although they do not allow their scale to be measured. In 1977 the anthropologist Michael Harner proposed that it responded to a lack of animal protein; Bernard Ortiz de Montellano and others criticized this, arguing that the Mexica diet was sufficient and that consumption was ritual and limited.

hechos/esclavitud-entre-los-mexicas/resu.texto: The tlacotin had lost their freedom through debt, by selling themselves or being sold by their parents in times of hunger, for crimes, or as tribute. They could own property and marry, their children were born free, and some recovered their freedom. There were slave markets, such as that of Azcapotzalco, and merchants bought slaves to offer them in sacrifice at certain festivals. After the conquest the Spaniards received slaves from Indigenous lords and enslaved war captives; the Crown prohibited this in 1530, allowed it again in 1534, and the New Laws of 1542 prohibited making new Indian slaves.

hechos/conquista-de-tlatelolco/titulo.texto: The Conquest of Tlatelolco by Tenochtitlan

hechos/conquista-de-tlatelolco/resumen.texto: Tlatelolco, founded by Mexica on a neighboring islet and famous for its great market, was subjugated by Axayácatl in 1473 after a conflict between the two cities; its ruler Moquíhuix died in the fighting, and Tenochtitlan imposed military governors and tribute on it. Tlatelolcan texts preserved resentment against the Tenochca, which shows in their own account of the Spanish conquest.

hechos/dedicacion-del-templo-mayor-1487/.texto: The Dedication of the Templo Mayor in 1487 and the Number of Its Victims

Ahuízotl dedicated an expansion of the Templo Mayor, begun by Tízoc, with a mass sacrifice of captives from his campaigns, to which he invited allied and enemy lords. Durán, who followed a lost Nahua source, gives 80,400 victims over four days; that figure would imply roughly fourteen sacrifices per minute, day and night. Ross Hassig considered it exaggerated and proposed a range of 10,000 to 80,400, and other authors believe the chronicles' figures were inflated in oral tradition; so far no remains have been found that would allow the victims of that ceremony to be counted.

hechos/inundacion-de-tenochtitlan-1500/t.texto: The Flood of Tenochtitlan Caused by Ahuízotl's Aqueduct

hechos/inundacion-de-tenochtitlan-1500/r.texto: Ahuízotl had water from the Acuecuexco spring, in Coyoacán, brought to Tenochtitlan by an aqueduct; according to Durán, the lord of Coyoacán warned him of the danger and was executed for it. The flow flooded the city, which had to be partly rebuilt, and the chronicles attribute to the flood an injury that may have contributed to the death of the tlatoani in 1502.

hechos/naufragio-de-1511/titulo.texto: The 1511 Shipwreck and the Spanish Captives of Yucatán

hechos/naufragio-de-1511/resumen.texto: A caravel sailing from Darién to Santo Domingo was wrecked in 1511, and about twenty survivors reached the coast of Yucatán in a boat. According to what Jerónimo de Aguilar later recounted, several were sacrificed and others died as slaves; he survived in the service of a Maya lord, and Gonzalo Guerrero joined the society of Chetumal. In 1519 Cortés rescued Aguilar on Cozumel.

hechos/expedicion-de-hernandez-de-cordob.texto: The Expedition of Francisco Hernández de Córdoba to Yucatán

In February 1517 three ships left Cuba with some 110 men, among them Bernal Díaz. At Cape Catoche they saw Maya stone cities for the first time and were attacked; at Champotón the Maya defeated them and killed much of the expedition, and the captain died of his wounds on the return. They took back to Cuba news of a rich, populous land and two captured Maya who later served as interpreters.

hechos/expedicion-de-grijalva/resumen.texto: With four ships and some 240 men, Grijalva sailed along Cozumel, the coast of Campeche, the Tabasco River that today bears his name, and the coast of Veracruz in 1518, where envoys of Moctezuma received him and exchanged gold for glass beads. The gold he took to Cuba led Diego Velázquez to organize a third expedition, which he entrusted to Hernán Cortés.

hechos/batalla-de-centla/titulo.texto: The Battle of Centla and the Handing Over of Malintzin

hechos/batalla-de-centla/resumen.texto: In March 1519 Cortés's men defeated the Chontal Maya of Potonchán, in Tabasco, thanks above all to horses and artillery. The defeated lords handed over gold, mantles and twenty women, among them Malintzin, who would become the interpreter of the conquest; Cortés founded the town of Santa María de la Victoria there.

hechos/fundacion-de-veracruz/titulo.texto: The Founding of Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz and the Scuttling of the Ships

hechos/fundacion-de-veracruz/resumen.texto: In 1519 Cortés's men founded the Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz, whose cabildo named him captain general and chief justice to free him from the authority of the governor of Cuba, Diego Velázquez. To keep Velázquez's supporters from returning to Cuba, Cortés had the ships beached and stripped; the account that he burned them is later. The town was moved twice before settling, by the end of the 16th century, on the site of the present port.

hechos/alianza-de-cempoala/titulo.texto: The Alliance of the Totonacs of Cempoala with Cortés

hechos/alianza-de-cempoala/resumen.texto: The lord of Cempoala, a Totonac capital subject to tribute by the Mexica, complained to Cortés about Moctezuma's tax collectors, who according to Bernal Díaz were carrying off his sons and daughters to sacrifice them. With Cortés's backing the Totonacs seized the tax collectors and rebelled, and they supplied porters and warriors for the march to Tenochtitlan. It was the first of the Indigenous alliances that made the conquest possible.

hechos/alianza-tlaxcalteca/titulo.texto: The War and Alliance between Tlaxcala and Cortés

hechos/alianza-tlaxcalteca/resumen.texto: In September 1519 the Tlaxcalans, led by Xicohténcatl the Younger, fought the Spaniards and their Totonac allies for several days without being able to defeat them. The lords of the four cabeceras then decided to ally with Cortés against the Mexica, their enemies of decades; after the Noche Triste they received the defeated Spaniards and contributed tens of thousands of warriors to the siege of Tenochtitlan. In return, Tlaxcala obtained exceptional privileges from the Crown: it was not granted in encomienda, received a coat of arms and the title of city in 1535, and its nobles kept local government.

hechos/matanza-de-cholula/resumen.texto: In October 1519, in Cholula, a major religious center allied with the Mexica, the Spaniards and their Tlaxcalan allies killed thousands of people, mostly nobles and warriors gathered in the temple courtyard, and sacked and burned the city. Cortés and Bernal Díaz say they acted ahead of an ambush prepared with Moctezuma's troops, which Malintzin had warned them of. Sahagún's informants and Las Casas, who was not there, present it as an unprovoked attack, and historians such as Ross Hassig believe the Tlaxcalans, enemies of Cholula, encouraged it. Cortés wrote that more than three thousand died in two hours; other sources give higher figures. It was one of the charges in his residencia trial.

hechos/prision-de-moctezuma/resumen.texto: A few days after entering Tenochtitlan, in November 1519, Cortés held Moctezuma in the palace of Axayácatl, where the Spaniards were lodged, on the pretext of an attack on Spaniards on the coast attributed to a Mexica lord, Cuauhpopoca, whom he had burned alive. For months Moctezuma continued to rule under custody. According to Cortés, he declared himself a vassal of Charles V; historians such as Matthew Restall consider this a construction by Cortés to give the conquest a legal form.

hechos/derrota-de-narvaez/resumen.texto: Diego Velázquez sent Pánfilo de Narváez with some 800 to 900 men to seize Cortés. Cortés left Pedro de Alvarado in Tenochtitlan with about a hundred Spaniards, marched to the coast, and at the end of May 1520 surprised Narváez at night in Cempoala, took him prisoner, and added his men, horses and weapons to his own. Smallpox had arrived with Narváez's fleet.

hechos/matanza-del-templo-mayor/titulo.texto: The Massacre at the Templo Mayor during the Tóxcatl Festival

hechos/matanza-del-templo-mayor/resumen.texto: In May 1520, while Cortés was on the coast, Mexica nobles and warriors were celebrating the Tóxcatl festival in the courtyard of the Templo Mayor with the permission of Pedro de Alvarado. The Spaniards closed the exits and attacked them while they danced, killing hundreds or thousands, according to the sources. Sahagún's informants recount it as a treacherous massacre; Alvarado claimed they were preparing an uprising for the end of the festival, and some historians believe he acted out of fear of an attack. The massacre provoked the city's rebellion, which besieged the Spaniards in their palace.

hechos/muerte-de-moctezuma/resumen.texto: In late June 1520, with the Spaniards besieged in Axayácatl's palace, Moctezuma died in circumstances that the sources recount in opposing ways. Cortés, Bernal Díaz and other Spaniards say that, while speaking from a rooftop to calm his people, he was struck by stones thrown by his own people and died days later. Sahagún's informants say the Spaniards threw his body out of the palace, and Durán, Ixtlilxóchitl and Chimalpahin maintain that the Spaniards killed him, by stabbing or strangling, before fleeing. Neither account can be confirmed, and both sides had reasons to blame the other.

hechos/noche-triste/resumen.texto: On the night of June 30 to July 1, 1520, the Spaniards and their Tlaxcalan allies tried to leave Tenochtitlan secretly by the Tlacopan causeway; discovered, they were attacked from canoes at the gaps in the causeway. Cortés admitted some 150 Spaniards and more than two thousand allies killed; Bernal Díaz, also counting the fighting of the following days, speaks of about 860 Spaniards. Nearly all the gold was lost, and the Spanish prisoners were sacrificed.

hechos/batalla-de-otumba/resumen.texto: On July 7, 1520, on the road to Tlaxcala, the Spaniards and Tlaxcalans who had survived the Noche Triste were overtaken by a large Mexica army on the plain of Otumba. According to Cortés and Bernal Díaz, they were saved when a cavalry charge knocked down the captain carrying the army's standard, which scattered the Mexica. They reached Tlaxcala, where they were received and were able to regroup.

hechos/epidemia-de-viruela-de-1520/resum.texto: Smallpox reached Mexico with Narváez's fleet in the spring of 1520; the chronicles attribute the contagion to an enslaved African in that expedition. It spread from Cempoala and between October and December struck Tenochtitlan for some sixty days: Sahagún's informants describe the sick covered in pustules, unable to move, dying of the disease and hunger. The tlatoani Cuitláhuac, the Tlaxcalan lord Maxixcatzin and a part of the population that cannot be calculated precisely died. It was the first of the great epidemics that, together with other causes, reduced the Indigenous population of Mexico in the 16th century.

hechos/campana-de-tepeaca/titulo.texto: The Tepeaca Campaign and the Branding of Slaves

hechos/campana-de-tepeaca/resumen.texto: Regrouped in Tlaxcala, Cortés and his allies attacked Tepeaca and other peoples allied with the Mexica between August and October 1520, accused of having killed Spaniards, and founded there the town of Segura de la Frontera. Cortés declared the prisoners slaves as punishment for their “rebellion” and had them branded with iron; Bernal Díaz recounts the branding and the soldiers' complaints because the captains kept the best women for themselves. The enslavement of captives from peoples considered rebellious was lawful for the Crown, except between 1530 and 1534, until the New Laws of 1542.

hechos/matanza-de-zultepec/resumen.texto: In 1520 the Acolhua people of Zultépec, subject to Texcoco, captured a caravan traveling from Veracruz to Tenochtitlan, carrying Spaniards, among them women, Africans and Indigenous allies, and sacrificed them. Cortés and Bernal Díaz recount that the Spaniards later found clothing, horse hides and an inscription written by one of the captives. Excavations by the INAH, directed from the 1990s by Enrique Martínez Vargas, found the remains of hundreds of people bearing marks of sacrifice and dismemberment, who were sacrificed over a period of months according to archaeologists. The site came to be called Tecoaque, “where they were eaten.” In 1521 Gonzalo de Sandoval punished the town.

hechos/bergantines-de-texcoco/resumen.texto: The carpenter Martín López directed the construction in Tlaxcala of thirteen brigantines, whose pieces were carried to Texcoco by thousands of Tlaxcalan porters. There they were assembled and, at the end of April 1521, launched onto the lake through a canal dug by thousands of Texcocan workers. With them the Spaniards controlled the lake during the siege and cut off Tenochtitlan’s water supply.

hechos/aliados-indigenas-de-la-conquista.texto: The Indigenous allies of the conquest and their numbers

According to Cortés, about 900 Spaniards with 86 horses and thirteen brigantines fought in the siege of Tenochtitlan, alongside armies from Tlaxcala, Texcoco, Huexotzinco, Cholula, Chalco and other peoples. The figures for allies given by the sources range from tens of thousands to more than a hundred thousand and cannot be verified: Cortés tended to minimize his own role, and the Tlaxcalan and Texcocan chroniclers to exalt the role of their city. Historians such as Ross Hassig, Matthew Restall and the authors of Indian Conquistadors argue that the conquest would not have been possible without them, and that many fought for their own interests, against Mexica domination or against local rivals.

hechos/sitio-de-tenochtitlan/titulo.texto: The siege of Tenochtitlan: hunger, sacrifices and massacres

hechos/sitio-de-tenochtitlan/resumen.texto: From late May 1521 the Spaniards and their allies cut the Chapultepec aqueduct and surrounded the city for about three months, by the causeways and with the brigantines. To advance, Cortés had the houses of the districts he took demolished and their canals filled in. The Anales de Tlatelolco and Sahagún’s informants describe the hunger, thirst and disease of the besieged. Bernal Díaz recounts that, after a failed assault at the end of June, they watched from their camp as the Mexica sacrificed dozens of their captured comrades at the Templo Mayor. About the final days, in Tlatelolco, Cortés wrote that in a single day more than forty thousand people were killed or captured, and that it was harder to restrain the cruelty of his Indigenous allies than to fight. None of the death tolls for the siege can be verified.

hechos/tortura-de-cuauhtemoc/resumen.texto: After the fall of Tenochtitlan, given the little gold recovered, the royal officials, in particular treasurer Julián de Alderete, pressed for Cuauhtémoc and the lord of Tlacopan to be interrogated under torture. According to Bernal Díaz and Gómara, Cortés consented, and their feet were burned with oil. Cuauhtémoc revealed little, and the torture was one of the charges against Cortés in his residencia trial. In those months, according to the Anales de Tlatelolco, three wise men of Texcoco who surrendered with their painted books were thrown to the dogs in Coyoacán. A 16th-century pictographic manuscript from Coyoacán, held at the Bibliothèque nationale de France, shows an Indigenous lord in chains being attacked by a dog.

hechos/mito-de-cortes-como-quetzalcoatl/.texto: The myth of Cortés as Quetzalcoatl

According to a widely repeated version, Moctezuma believed that Cortés was the god Quetzalcoatl returning from the east, and a series of omens announced the fall of the city. Cortés attributed to Moctezuma a speech in which he recognized the king of Spain as heir of an ancient lord who had departed. Historians such as Matthew Restall consider this an invention to lend legality to the conquest. The identification with Quetzalcoatl and the omens appear only in the Florentine Codex and in other works written decades later. Susan Gillespie, Camilla Townsend and Restall consider it a construction made after the conquest, which explained the defeat as the fulfillment of a prophecy.

hechos/sujecion-de-michoacan/titulo.texto: The subjugation of the Purépecha kingdom
