hechos/sujecion-de-michoacan/resumen.texto: After the fall of Tenochtitlan, the cazonci Tangáxoan, whose father had died of smallpox in 1520, accepted in 1522 the entry of Cristóbal de Olid into Tzintzuntzan and submitted without war. The Spaniards carried off the royal treasure and stripped the temples. Michoacán was divided into encomiendas, and the Franciscans began evangelization.

hechos/ejecucion-de-cuauhtemoc/resumen.texto: In February 1525, during Cortés’s march to Honduras to punish the rebellion of Cristóbal de Olid, Cuauhtémoc, Tetlepanquetzal and other lords he held as hostages were accused, on the denunciation of a Mexica nobleman, of conspiring to kill the Spaniards. They were hanged in the province of Acalan. Cortés justified it in his fifth letter. Bernal Díaz, who was on the expedition, wrote that it was an unjust death that displeased everyone who was on the journey.

hechos/ejecucion-del-cazonci/titulo.texto: The execution of the cazonci by Nuño de Guzmán

hechos/ejecucion-del-cazonci/resumen.texto: In February 1530, at the start of his campaign to the west, Nuño de Guzmán took the cazonci with him and had him tortured, together with his close associates, to make him hand over gold. He was then subjected to a summary trial for idolatry, the deaths of Spaniards and an alleged conspiracy. He was condemned and executed in Guzmán’s camp by the Lerma River, and his body was burned. Michoacán was left without its ruler and in years of violence, until the second Audiencia sent the oidor Vasco de Quiroga to visit it in 1533.

hechos/conquista-de-nueva-galicia/titulo.texto: The conquest of New Galicia by Nuño de Guzmán

hechos/conquista-de-nueva-galicia/resume.texto: At the end of 1529 Nuño de Guzmán left Mexico for the west with some four hundred Spaniards and thousands of Indigenous warriors from the center and from Michoacán. Over two years he traversed present-day Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa with massacres, burned villages, torture and the enslavement of captives, documented by witnesses from his own side and by his rivals. He named the region New Galicia and founded towns such as Compostela and Guadalajara. The violence and the encomiendas that followed were causes of the Mixtón War.

hechos/guerra-del-mixton/resumen.texto: In 1540 the Caxcanes and other peoples of New Galicia, punished by the violence of the conquest and by the encomiendas, rose in a religious movement that announced the expulsion of the Spaniards. They entrenched themselves on rocky hilltops (peñoles) such as Mixtón and Nochistlán. They killed encomenderos and friars, defeated several expeditions, in one of which Pedro de Alvarado died (1541), and attacked Guadalajara. Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza led a campaign in 1541–1542 with some 450 Spaniards and tens of thousands of Nahua, Tlaxcalan and Purépecha warriors, which took the peñoles. Thousands of rebels died and many captives were enslaved. The executions ordered by the viceroy were one of the charges in the visita of Francisco Tello de Sandoval.

hechos/colonias-tlaxcaltecas-del-norte/t.texto: The Tlaxcalan colonies of the north

hechos/colonias-tlaxcaltecas-del-norte/r.texto: In 1591, to end the Chichimec War with gifts, missions and settlements (the “peace by purchase,” in the words of historian Philip Powell), Viceroy Luis de Velasco the Younger agreed with Tlaxcala to move some 400 Tlaxcalan families to the northern frontier. In exchange they received privileges such as hidalgo status, their own lands, exemption from tribute and a ban on Spaniards living in their towns. They founded or settled neighborhoods next to Saltillo, San Luis Potosí, Colotlán and other places, with the stated aim that they would serve the Chichimecs as a model of a Christian, agricultural town.

hechos/conquista-de-yucatan/resumen.texto: Yucatán had no central state but more than fifteen rival Maya lordships, which made the conquest slow. Francisco de Montejo’s campaigns between 1527 and 1535 failed. His son and nephew resumed it in 1540 with the alliance of the Xiu of Maní, founded Campeche and Mérida (1542), and subjugated the north around 1545. In 1546–1547 a great rebellion in the east was suppressed harshly. The conquest brought encomiendas, forced labor and, in 1562, Diego de Landa’s campaign against idolatry. In 1552 the oidor Tomás López Medel issued ordinances on tribute, labor and the government of the Maya towns to limit the abuses of the encomenderos. The south, with the Itzá, remained independent until 1697.

hechos/fundacion-de-merida-yucatan/titul.texto: The founding of Mérida on T'ho

hechos/fundacion-de-merida-yucatan/resum.texto: On January 6, 1542 Francisco de Montejo the Younger founded Mérida on the Maya city of T'ho. Its stone buildings reminded the Spaniards of the Roman ruins of Mérida, in Extremadura, and the stones of its pyramids were used for the cathedral and Spanish houses. Shortly afterward the lord of Maní, of the Xiu, presented himself in peace before the Montejos.

hechos/rebelion-maya-de-1546/resumen.texto: In November 1546 the lordships of eastern Yucatán, led by the Cupul and the Cocom, rose against the encomenderos. They killed Spaniards, Maya who served them and their animals, and besieged Valladolid. The Montejos suppressed the rebellion in about four months with Spanish troops and Maya allies. Spanish chroniclers describe the torture death of captured Spaniards, and the repression included executions and the enslavement of prisoners.

hechos/conquista-de-tayasal/titulo.texto: The fall of Nojpetén, the last Maya kingdom

hechos/conquista-de-tayasal/resumen.texto: The Itzá kept their independent kingdom for almost two centuries after the fall of Tenochtitlan. Cortés passed through there in 1525, and several Franciscan missions failed in the 17th century. After negotiations with Ajaw Kan Ek’ did not succeed, on March 13, 1697 the troops of Martín de Ursúa attacked the island from a galleot and took it in a few hours, with many Itzá killed in the water. They destroyed the temples. Epidemics, war and flight into the forest greatly reduced the population in the following years.

hechos/hallazgo-de-la-piedra-del-sol/tit.texto: The discovery of the Coatlicue and the Sun Stone

hechos/hallazgo-de-la-piedra-del-sol/res.texto: In 1790, during leveling work in the main plaza of Mexico City, the great sculpture of the goddess Coatlicue and the Sun Stone came to light. Antonio de León y Gama studied them in a book of 1792, one of the first archaeological studies in the Americas. The Coatlicue was buried again in the courtyard of the University for fear that it would encourage its cult, and it was dug up in the 19th century.

hechos/proyecto-templo-mayor/titulo.texto: The discovery of Coyolxauhqui and the Templo Mayor Project

hechos/proyecto-templo-mayor/resumen.texto: On February 21, 1978 workers from the electricity company found a large monolith of the dismembered goddess Coyolxauhqui in the center of Mexico City. The INAH then began, under the direction of Eduardo Matos Moctezuma, the excavation of the Templo Mayor. It required the demolition of several buildings in the area and revealed seven construction phases and more than a hundred offerings. Since 1991 it has been directed by Leonardo López Luján. In 2006 the monolith of Tlaltecuhtli was found, the largest known Mexica sculpture.

hechos/hallazgo-del-huey-tzompantli/titu.texto: The discovery of the Huey Tzompantli

hechos/hallazgo-del-huey-tzompantli/resu.texto: Since 2015 the Urban Archaeology Program of the INAH, directed by Raúl Barrera, has excavated part of the Huey Tzompantli under a house on República de Guatemala Street, behind the Cathedral. It is the platform where the skulls of the sacrificed were displayed on beams, and a circular tower of skulls joined with lime. By 2017, 676 skulls had been recorded there, and in 2020 another 119. The analyses showed a majority of young men, but also women and children, which contradicts the idea that only warriors were displayed. It confirms the structure described by Andrés de Tapia and other conquistadors. Their figure of 136,000 skulls remains unverified.

hechos/restos-de-ixcateopan/titulo.texto: The alleged remains of Cuauhtémoc in Ixcateopan

hechos/restos-de-ixcateopan/resumen.texto: In 1949 the historian Eulalia Guzmán announced that she had found, under the altar of the church in Ixcateopan, Guerrero, the remains of Cuauhtémoc, along with documents that asserted it. Commissions of specialists convened in 1949–1951 and in 1976 concluded that the bones belonged to several people and that the documents were recent forgeries. Sixteenth-century sources say that Cuauhtémoc died in Acalan, hundreds of kilometers away. Even so, the site remains a place of official commemoration.

hechos/expedicion-a-las-hibueras/resumen.texto: In October 1524 Cortés left Mexico for Honduras to punish the rebellion of Cristóbal de Olid, with some hundreds of Spaniards, thousands of Indigenous warriors and porters, and the Mexica lords as hostages. The march through the jungles and swamps of Tabasco, Acalan and Petén was disastrous. Many of the Indigenous companions died of hunger and disease, Cuauhtémoc was hanged in Acalan, and in 1525 the Spaniards passed through Nojpetén, the Itzá capital. Cortés recounted it in his fifth letter and returned to Mexico in 1526.

lugares/templo-mayor/resumen.texto: Twin pyramid dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and Tláloc at the center of the sacred precinct of Tenochtitlan, with seven main construction phases between the founding of the city and 1521. The city’s principal sacrifices were held there, and facing it stood the Huey Tzompantli. The Spaniards demolished it after the conquest and used its stones in the new city. Since 1978 it has been excavated, and it has a museum next to the Cathedral.

lugares/tlatelolco/resumen.texto: Twin city of Tenochtitlan, founded by the Mexica on a neighboring islet and famous for its market, which Cortés and Bernal Díaz described with astonishment. It was subjugated by Tenochtitlan in 1473 and was the last redoubt of the defense in 1521. Afterward the Franciscan convent of Santiago and the College of Santa Cruz, where the Florentine Codex was produced, operated there. The Plaza de las Tres Culturas preserves its ruins.

lugares/texcoco/resumen.texto: City of the Acolhua on the eastern shore of the lake, second in importance in the Aztec Triple Alliance, and court of Nezahualcóyotl and Nezahualpilli. Divided by the succession of 1515, part of its nobility allied with Cortés, who built the brigantines for the siege of Tenochtitlan there. It was the seat of one of the first Franciscan schools in New Spain.

lugares/tlaxcala/resumen.texto: Capital of the Tlaxcalan lordship, formed by four head towns (cabeceras) on the hills by the Zahuapan River, independent of the Triple Alliance and allied with Cortés since 1519. In the 1520s the colonial city was laid out in the valley, with one of the first Franciscan convents and the first seat of the bishopric of Tlaxcala, which was moved to Puebla in 1543. Its Indigenous cabildo governed with the privileges of an allied city of the Crown.

lugares/tizatlan/resumen.texto: One of the four head towns of Tlaxcala, seat of Xicohténcatl the Elder. It preserves the remains of a palace with altars painted with gods and ritual scenes in the style of the codices, and a 16th-century open-air Franciscan chapel.

lugares/veracruz/resumen.texto: Port founded by Cortés’s men in 1519 as Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz. It was moved twice before settling, at the end of the 16th century, opposite the island of San Juan de Ulúa. Throughout the colonial period it was New Spain’s main port with Europe, the arrival point of the fleets and of the trade in enslaved Africans.

lugares/cempoala/resumen.texto: Totonac capital on the coastal plain of Veracruz, with temples on platforms and walled enclosures, the first great city the Spaniards saw on the mainland. Its lord allied with Cortés in 1519, and Narváez was defeated there in 1520. Epidemics depopulated it in the 16th century.

lugares/tecoaque/resumen.texto: Acolhua settlement near Calpulalpan, in Tlaxcala, where in 1520 a caravan of Spaniards and their companions was captured and sacrificed. Excavated by the INAH since the 1990s, it preserves temples, houses and storehouses with the remains of the captives.

lugares/malinalco/resumen.texto: Religious center conquered by the Mexica in the time of Axayácatl, in present-day State of Mexico. It preserves a temple carved into the living rock of the hill, with sculptures of eagles and jaguars, associated with the Mexica military orders and built in the last years before the conquest.

lugares/texcotzingo/resumen.texto: Hill near Texcoco where Nezahualcóyotl had gardens, terraces, baths carved into the rock and an aqueduct built that brought water from the mountains. They are known as the baths of Nezahualcóyotl.

lugares/nojpeten/resumen.texto: Capital of the Itzá kingdom, on an island in Lake Petén Itzá, in northern Guatemala. It was the last great independent Maya center until the Spanish assault of March 13, 1697. The city of Flores stands on the site today.

lugares/merida-yucatan/resumen.texto: City founded in 1542 by Francisco de Montejo the Younger on the Maya city of T'ho, capital of the governorship of Yucatán. Its cathedral, completed in 1598, was built partly with stones from the ancient Maya buildings.

lugares/campeche/resumen.texto: Port founded by Francisco de Montejo the Younger around 1540, next to the Maya town of Ah Kin Pech, and base of the conquest of Yucatán. Because of pirate attacks in the 16th and 17th centuries it was walled, and its walls are a World Heritage Site.

lugares/tenayuca/resumen.texto: Former capital of the Chichimecs of Xólotl according to Texcocan chronicles, north of the Valley of Mexico. Its pyramid, enlarged several times and surrounded by a wall of stone serpents, has the same double-temple model that the Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan later had.

lugares/xochimilco/resumen.texto: Nahuatl-speaking lordship on the southern shore of the lake, subjugated by the Mexica in the time of Itzcóatl and famous for its chinampas. The chinampas are still cultivated and have been a World Heritage Site since 1987, together with the historic center of Mexico City.

lugares/chapultepec/resumen.texto: Hill by the lake where the Mexica settled during their migration and from which, according to their chronicles, their neighbors expelled them at the end of the 13th century. From the 15th century an aqueduct carried its fresh water to Tenochtitlan, and the tlatoque had their portraits carved into the rock there. Today it is a large park in Mexico City.

lugares/palacio-de-cortes-cuernavaca/res.texto: Fortified residence that Hernán Cortés had built with Indigenous labor in the 1520s on the platform of a Tlahuica temple in Cuauhnáhuac, center of his marquisate of the Valley of Oaxaca. It is now a museum and preserves Diego Rivera’s 1930 murals on the conquest.
